Exelby, which has just now become the property of the house, provides evidence that in his statement on March 8, as reported at page 2783 of Hansard, the Minister of Labour misinformed and misled the house with respect to a matter coming under his jurisdiction as a minister responsible to this house.

It seems to me that the hon. member is endeavouring to challenge what the minister said. If there is a misleading of the house by an hon. member or a minister, and it is an intentional misleading, it will undoubtedly raise a question for consideration by the house, using the proper procedure. That the matter of the statements of the Minister of Labour in this house with regard to the case of Mr. Glen H. Exelby together with the sworn statement by Mr. Exelby tabled today be referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections for appropriate action.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  MOTION TO REFER EXELBY MATTER TO COMMITTEE

prima facie question of privilege arise on the allegation by the hon. member that the minister has misinformed the house?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: Once again today an attempt is being made to upset the regular business of the house. I think this is the first time an attempt of this kind has been made in the 25 years I have been a member of the House of Commons. Just to show how ridiculous it is, let me remind hon. members that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate had a copy of this affidavit yesterday. He told us he had received a copy or, in any event, it was common ground that he had one. The question was discussed yesterday. If he was going to raise a question of privilege, that was the time when it should have been done.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  MOTION TO REFER EXELBY MATTER TO COMMITTEE
speechtext: It had not even been tabled then.

speechtext: There was no need for it to be tabled, as the hon. member had it in his own possession. Surely he is not at liberty to come in today and initiate a question of privilege of this kind. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  MOTION TO REFER EXELBY MATTER TO COMMITTEE
speechtext: The question I have to determine and with regard to which I am seeking the assistance of the Acting Prime Minister is whether or not the circumstances which have been alleged amount to a prima facie breach of the privileges of the house. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  MOTION TO REFER EXELBY MATTER TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
To put the situation in its very worst aspect, here you have a case where an affidavit by an interested party is produced and an attempt is made to use that against the word which the Minister of Labour gave to the house. I suggest it is stretching things very far if a member of the opposition can go out and get an affidavit from someone whose name has been mentioned in the house and then come in and use that affidavit as part of an attempt to bring in a motion on a question of privilege as a means of attacking statements made by responsible ministers. I suggest that this is going entirely too far, and if we are to have orderly conduct of the business of this house we should be going ahead with the work of parliament and not have these red herrings thrown in every day.
Hon. gentlemen opposite had the opportunity to discuss this question when the estimates of the Department of Labour were up for consideration last week. They have

brought it up on every possible occasion, doing their best to wring the last bit of publicity out of the question, and I suggest that when they bring in this motion today they are going too far.

speechtext: Perhaps I may speak on this question, because it directly affects me. The statement I made in this house was based on information, and correct information, which was supplied to me by the national employment service office, information which I disclosed in this house.

speechtext: Contrary to the law.

Well, we know that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is a real expert on everything. I do not purport to be so.
May I call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that there is on the order paper under notices of motion for production of papers a motion, No. 82, which asks for a copy of all the records in this case. Yesterday I asked that this motion should stand until Wednesday when, I said, it would be dealt with. In the circumstances I suggest that the present motion is premature until it has been proven that what I said in this house, based on the information I got from the national employment office, was incorrect. If these papers and records are produced they will substantiate whether the information I got was true or false.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  MOTION TO REFER EXELBY MATTER TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, surely the raising of a question of privilege in the house is analogous to contempt of court, and there is nothing similar to that at all in the present circumstances. Beauchesne states examples of what are regarded as breaches of privilege in citation 111. They include reflections on the character of the Speaker, reflections upon the conduct of the chairman of committees, imputing unfair conduct to the chairman of a select committee and imputations against members of corruption in the execution of their duties.
That surely is what constitutes a breach of the privilege of the house, something analogous to contempt of court. Surely if the hon. member in question is not entitled to impugn the accuracy of information given to the house by a minister he is not going to accomplish the same purpose in this indirect and clandestine way.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  MOTION TO REFER EXELBY MATTER TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
As I understand it we are discussing whether there is a prima facie question of privilege. We are seeking to assist Your Honour in reaching a conclusion about that matter. The only argument advanced by the Acting Prime Minister against my contention that there is, is that this

matter could have been raised yesterday. I do not think it could have been raised yesterday because the document on which it is based was not in the possession of the house then. It is quite true that I had a copy of the document, but I did not have the original; it was sent to the Minister of Labour. Moreover, sir, I felt it would be improper for me, inside or outside the house, to do anything about that document until the Minister of Labour had the opportunity, which he was given yesterday afternoon in this house, to make amends, an opportunity which he did not take.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

Instead of which the
minister undertook to summarize the document, leaving out important portions of it. That is surely something about which the minister does not want to have left any doubt whatsoever.
The motion I am making is a motion to follow the procedure of this house to clear up the matter. The Acting Prime Minister said that in the 25 years he had been in this house no such motion had been made before. Well, I do not know where the minister was last year when the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) raised a motion of a similar character about a much less important matter. Moreover, Your Honour recognized the privilege by implication on March 9 when I raised an earlier question of privilege, which will be found at page 2811 of Hansard with respect to this same statement by the minister. Your Honour said:
The hon. member tor Bonavista-Twillingate has risen on a matter of privilege. The point he makes is that a minister of the crown in the house has not observed the conditions of a statute passed by the house. I think a matter of privilege properly arises under such circumstances-
Surely, sir, if you felt that a matter of privilege properly arose under that kind of circumstance, when at that time we had reason to think what the minister had said was correct, it arises doubly when a man makes a sworn statement-which would constitute perjury if it were not true-that
Question of Privilege
what the minister said is not true and that this house has been misinformed.
Of course, sir, this is not the only evidence. The evidence of the actual employer of this man and the evidence of someone to whom he applied for a job is to the same effect as the evidence given by Mr. Exelby. All these witnesses point to the untruth of two statements made in this house by the minister on March 8. It seems to me, sir, that there is only one proper way to clean it up. Moreover, if Your Honour will refer to paragraph 108 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms already quoted by the learned and hon. member for Stormont-

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  MOTION TO REFER EXELBY MATTER TO COMMITTEE
speechtext: I will be brief, Mr. Speaker. This house is frequently misinformed and misled. No question of privilege arises unless it is intentional. I do not admit for one moment that the house has been misinformed or misled in this instance, but no allegation has been made that it was intentional nor could one be made. Therefore there can be no question of privilege.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  MOTION TO REFER EXELBY MATTER TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I wonder if I might draw Your Honour's attention to Beauchesne's fourth edition, page 102, paragraph 113, half way down, where it states as follows:
But a dispute arising between two members, as to allegations of facts, does not fulfil the conditions of parliamentary privilege.
I suggest to you that this is a dispute originated by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who has declined to accept the

Question of Privilege
statement of the Minister of Labour and then on the basis of an affidavit or a statement, or both, made outside the house has attempted to launch here a question of privilege and a reference to a committee.
In his motion also, Mr. Speaker, I point out that he does not make any point of privilege whatsoever. He is so unsure of his facts that all he asks is that these matters be referred to a committee. He has nothing on which to found his statement or his motion would disclose that fact. He is simply asking for an investigation by a committee, yet in so far as the house is concerned the Minister of Labour has placed on record the facts that were in his possession, and his statement as to the validity and the truth of those facts should be accepted. That is the normal practice of this house.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  MOTION TO REFER EXELBY MATTER TO COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I say a word about the point just raised by the house leader?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  MOTION TO REFER EXELBY MATTER TO COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order. If the hon. member who raises this matter wishes to reply to the statement of the house leader, I think I will hear him before I dispose of the matter.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  MOTION TO REFER EXELBY MATTER TO COMMITTEE
speechtext: I just want to say a word regarding the form of the motion and to draw Your Honour's attention to the fact that in seeking the proper form for my motion I was guided by the advice your honour gave to the hon. member for Timmins on a question of privilege which arose last year.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  MOTION TO REFER EXELBY MATTER TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Order. I feel that no good purpose would be served by further argument as to whether there is a matter of privilege.
There are two points made regarding the matter raised by the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate. The first is that there has been delay in raising the matter. The statement of the minister complained of was made, I believe, last week and the reason for questioning that statement which has been given today by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is an affidavit which was referred to yesterday and which the minister was asked to table and has tabled now, and which I think the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate acknowledges he had in his possession yesterday at the time the Minister of Labour made a second statement, although not the original affidavit.
I doubt that I would dispose of the matter on the ground of delay alone, although it is important that questions of privilege should be dealt with when they arise.
The other point, which I think is made most effectively by the house leader, is that there should be more involved than a dispute between two members as to facts. One has to distinguish between the privileges of the

house and privileges of individual members. I see nothing that involves the rights or privileges of the individual member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who raised the matter. If there is any proper complaint for the house to raise against the minister it is based on his conduct in supplying information to the house.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate alleges that the information supplied by the minister was not true according to the affidavit in question. If, on nothing further, the house were to accept those circumstances as raising a prima facie question of privilege, it would be very difficult to conduct business in the house because almost any statement that is made by any member or minister could be disputed in some form or other by affidavit or contrary evidence.
Beauchesne recognizes that problem in citation 113, which was cited to me. It appears in Beauchesne's fourth edition at page 102, where he says that a dispute arising between two members, as to allegations of facts, does not fulfil the conditions of parliamentary privilege. I feel there is a necessary element lacking in the case made by the hon. member. I feel that he should have been prepared, if he wished to found a motion on his statement, to allege that there was bad faith on the part of the minister; that he deliberately supplied the house with wrong information. That would to my mind, raise a question of privilege of the house. But in the circumstance of a dispute arising over statements made by the minister in the course of his duty or, for that matter, by any member in his place making statements on his responsibility as a member of the house, one has to remember that the whole of parliamentary procedure is really based on the disputing of such statements in debate. Unless it goes beyond debate, in that sort of dispute, I feel that I would be leading the house into interminable difficulties if I accepted this circumstance as it is before us now as raising a matter of privilege sufficient to found a motion which does not allege that there was in fact a deliberate misleading of the house by the Minister of Labour.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  MOTION TO REFER EXELBY MATTER TO COMMITTEE
speechtext: I should like to leave no doubt on that point. It is my opinion that there was a deliberate misleading of the house.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

low as to even think, as the hon. member does, that other hon. members do so deliberately.

point of privilege, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I have been in this house only a short

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacLean (Minister of Fisheries) moved
subtopic: REVISION OF DEFINITION OF CANADIAN FISHING VESSEL
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-57 to amend the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is very short and straightforward. By way of explanation I may say that the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act was last revised in 1953. The main purpose of the act is to protect fisheries in Canadian territorial waters against encroachment by foreign fishing vessels and to regulate the privileges accorded to foreign fishing vessels in our ports.
Subject to any treaty rights, the act prohibits fishing operations by foreign fishing vessels in our waters. A foreign fishing vessel is defined in the act as a fishing vessel that is not a Canadian fishing vessel. The same section defines what constitutes a Canadian fishing vessel. There are four requirements listed in the act as it now stands, and I think the intention was that in order to be considered a Canadian fishing vessel, a vessel


had to meet one of these main requirements. Under the law as it presently stands, any fishing vessel which satisfies one of the four chief requirements which I have mentioned is a Canadian fishing vessel within the meaning of the act. That is to say, a vessel registered in a foreign country but owned in Canada would, under the present definition, be considered a Canadian vessel.
In recent years there has been a significant increase in fishing operations in the high seas adjacent to Canadian territorial waters. It is therefore necessary for the protection of Canadian fisheries to clarify the law so as to make sure that before a fishing vessel can be considered a Canadian fishing vessel, and consequently entitled to operate in Canadian waters, it must be registered or licensed in Canada and owned in Canada; or, in the case of fishing vessels which are not required under Canadian law to be registered, that is to say small boats, that they be owned in Canada and not registered elsewhere.
There is nothing complicated or obscure about the amendment. It is intended purely to clarify this section of the act which defines what is meant by a Canadian fishing vessel. There are no other implications in the amendment at all.

subtopic: REVISION OF DEFINITION OF CANADIAN FISHING VESSEL
speechtext:
I wish to thank the minister for the brief explanation he has given of the amendment now before the house for consideration. As the minister said, its purpose is to clarify the definition of a Canadian fishing vessel. The hon. gentleman made reference to the purpose of the fisheries protection act, and he also referred to encroachment by foreign fishing vessels which are operating in proximity to our Canadian shores.
I feel that the minister is missing a golden opportunity to amend this act so as to provide proper protection for Canadian fishermen. Under the present regulations as they affect our territorial and coastal waters, foreign vessels are allowed to fish up to three miles from our shores although certain of our own Canadian vessels, vessels of a certain size, cannot come within ten miles of our shores. I recall very well that in years past, when some of the hon. members who are now sitting on the government side of this house were members of the opposition, they took the opportunity provided by consideration of the estimates of the Department of Fisheries to advise the government how it should proceed in order to remedy this most unfortunate situation. I know, and everyone knows, that in the last three years very little if anything has been done to change the position.
We understand that the present amendment will to some extent clarify the definition of

what is a Canadian fishing vessel. But let us look carefully at the amendment, particularly as it is set out in subparagraph (a) which is now to read:
"Canadian fishing vessel" means a fishing vessel
(i)	that is registered or licensed in Canada under the Canada Shipping Act and is owned by one or more persons each of whom is a Canadian citizen, an individual resident in Canada or a corporation incorporated under the laws of Canada or of a province, having its principal place of business in Canada.
Under the old provision it is stated that a Canadian fishing vessel means a fishing vessel that is:
(i)	registered in Canada
(ii)	owned by one person domiciled and resident in Canada
-and so on. Under the present amendment the word "domiciled" has been taken out and replaced by "resident" only. It seems that under this definition, instead of restricting the interpretation of what is meant by a Canadian fishing vessel we have broadened it.
I repeat that I feel the minister has missed a golden opportunity to improve the position of Canadian fishermen vis-a-vis foreign fishing vessels. As far as I can see now, apart from what has been mentioned with regard to clause 1, all this amendment does is to bring within the definition of Canadian fishing vessels certain small boats which are not mechanically propelled and which, under the present regulation, could not be defined as Canadian fishing vessels.
It is an amendment of very minor significance, as the minister has said. I hope that later on this session when we shall be better able, under the rules of order, to discuss this section of the act in greater detail so far as it relates to the operation of draggers and other foreign fishing vessels operating in proximity to our Canadian shores, we shall be able to get from the minister a definite statement clarifying the policy of the present government so far as the operation of foreign owned fishing vessels is concerned within certain limits of our territorial waters.
When the present bill comes before the committee of the whole we shall be able to discuss the proposed amendment in greater detail, and I hope the minister at that time will be in a position to give us further information.

subtopic: REVISION OF DEFINITION OF CANADIAN FISHING VESSEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise to speak briefly on this bill to amend the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act. I wish first to commend the minister for the interest he has shown in all matters pertaining to his department, and especially for the action he has taken which will strengthen the position of the Canadian fisheries.
I also listened with much interest to the remarks made by the two previous speakers, the hon. members for Gloucester and Skeena, with respect to the three-mile limit versus the 12-mile limit. I consider it unfortunate that when the Liberals were in power the hon. member for Gloucester was not more vocal on this matter, which is of vital importance to fishermen on the east coast. I trust that the hon. member will contain his curiosity for a little longer this session, because I am hopeful that before long he will receive answers to some of the questions he has raised.
Originally the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act was designed to protect the fisheries in Canadian territorial waters from encroachment by foreign fishing vessels, and also to regulate the privileges accorded to foreign fishing vessels in our ports. Under the old act it was possible to have a vessel, registered in a foreign country but owned in Canada, considered a Canadian fishing vessel. Conversely, it was also possible to have a vessel registered in Canada owned by a resident who was not a Canadian citizen, and this ship was also classed as a Canadian fishing vessel. However, in recent years there has been a significant increase in fishing operations on the

Coastal Fisheries Protection Act
high seas adjacent to our territorial waters. Probably no other country in the world has the complex problems in fisheries management that confront Canada. Our interests on the east coast extend from Georges and Brown's bank, which lie in an easterly direction from Cape Sable, past LaHave bank, Emerald bank, Sable Island bank, Middle Ground, Canso bank, Banquereau, Misaine bank, St. Pierre bank, Green bank, the Great bank off Newfoundland to the fishing grounds off Labrador in the Labrador sea.
Our species range from lobsters and scallops to cod, haddock, pollack, halibut, flounder and almost every known kind of groundfish. Each area and species presents its own special problems requiring individual study and individual solutions, if indeed solutions in some cases exist. The tremendous resources of the sea made their contribution to bringing about the early development of the Atlantic provinces, especially Nova Scotia, and a study of early history will indicate the importance of the fisheries even in the days of Sir John A. Macdonald when negotiating with the United States. Even today the fishing industry in the Atlantic provinces is a potent force in our area's economy, with the commercial value of fish landed in the four Atlantic provinces during the year 1960 amounting to $59,891,000 in payments to the fishermen.
Our problem today when considering fisheries management and assistance to Canadian fishermen does not concern itself only with the protection of fish but also with the creation of conditions under which the entire resource can be maintained or improved for the benefit of Canada and for future generations of Canadians.
The world-wide interest in the ocean and its resources is becoming broadly apparent, and this is not difficult to understand. Resource competition among nations is becoming increasingly intensive, and with the exception of our narrow three-mile territorial fringe, the ocean resources are free. The fish are there for the taking on a first come, first served basis, and we are only now beginning to realize the value of this resource when we see the extravagant claims for expanded territorial seas put forward by certain nations desirous of protecting their fisheries, as well as the oil or mineral rights found on the continental shelf. However, as fishermen, we are mainly concerned with the ocean as a source of food supply; and as the world's population grows, with greater need for living space and less arable land to provide food, greater and still greater emphasis will be placed upon our fisheries to provide highly edible protein.

With these thoughts in mind, therefore, it becomes vitally important and necessary to tighten up the regulations dealing with Canadian fishing vessels. In my opinion these amendments will clarify the law so as to make certain that before a fishing vessel can be considered a Canadian fishing vessel and consequently entitled to operate in Canadian waters, it must be registered or licensed in Canada and owned in Canada by one or more persons each of whom is a Canadian citizen. While I believe still further changes are required for the protection of the rights of Canadian fishermen, these amendments are indeed a forward step and one in the right direction.

subtopic: REVISION OF DEFINITION OF CANADIAN FISHING VESSEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, any act that pertains to fisheries and particularly to fisheries protection is of special interest to Newfoundland. This bill will probably affect our province more than any other province in Canada.
If we look back over the history of legislation for the protection of fisheries, we find that there have been very few amendments since 1868 when the first law came into existence. It was entitled the customs and fisheries protection act. As we follow the history of the amendments that have been made we notice that practically all of them have resulted from an effort to expand or clarify the definition of a fishing vessel. The 1868 act lasted right up to 1913, when it was amended to define foreign vessels. In the 1913 act a foreign vessel was described as one which is not navigated according to the laws of the United Kingdom or of Canada. This amendment, of course, preserved the treaty rights which Canada had with the United States, as the government was empowered to allow United States vessels to enter Atlantic ports to purchase bait, lines, outfits and so forth.
In 1952 fisheries protection was separated from customs protection, and the definition of a fishing vessel was further enlarged to include sealing vessels, vessels engaged in the taking of marine plants and also processing vessels which are sometimes referred to as mother ships. The 1952 amendment was also necessary to legalize certain traditional privileges and arrangements between Newfoundland and foreign powers, for entry to Newfoundland ports, which were of long standing and which applied particularly to Portugal and Spain.
The definition of a fishing vessel under the present act is as follows:
(a) "Canadian fishing vessel" means a fishing vessel that is
(i) registered in Canada,

(ii)	owned by one person domiciled and resident in Canada,
(iii)	owned by two or more persons, all of whom are domiciled and resident in Canada, or
(iv)	owned by a body corporate incorporated under the laws of Canada or the laws of a province and having its principal place of business in Canada;-
The bill before us seeks to amend this definition in three important respects. For example, the first condition that a vessel must be registered in Canada is now enlarged to include registered or licensed in Canada. Condition No. 2, that a vessel must be owned by one person domiciled and resident in Canada, has been changed to just resident in Canada. The requirement to be domiciled has been eliminated. Condition No. 3, that a vessel must be owned by two or more persons, all of whom are domiciled and resident in Canada, has now been changed to eliminate the domiciliary requirement and to require the owners to be Canadian citizens. There is also a new paragraph which, as the hon. member for Gloucester pointed out, brings under this act those small ships which are not mechanically propelled and are not required to be licensed under the Canada Shipping Act.
These proposed amendments appear to involve a relaxation of the requirements of ownership which has been brought about by a broadening of the definition. In my opinion the omission of the word "domiciled" makes the definition much more vague than it was before, because the word "domiciled" has a very clear, precise meaning. When we eliminate this word and rely on the definition of being resident in Canada, the definition becomes somewhat blurred because the word "resident" unlike the word "domiciled" has no clear and fixed meaning. It has different meanings in different acts of parliament; it has different meanings in different parts of Canada and in different situations.
I can perhaps understand that there would be some advantages in having such a broad definition. I can see that perhaps it might facilitate deep-sea sportmen who come to Canada and spend a few weeks in some of our Atlantic ports fishing for tuna and indulging in that kind of sport fishing. But if on the other hand we regard the definition of fixed residence as important, then it seems that the use of the word "resident" when dissociated from the word "domiciled" may constitute a loophole which could be taken advantage of and, as the hon. member for Skeena pointed out, it may not achieve the purpose that we intend this legislation to accomplish.
I suggest that the minister might consider writing a definition into this act so that we would know exactly what the word "resident"
Coastal Fisheries Protection Act means as it applies to this particular legislation. It was not possible to do this in the 1913 act because that act included vessels from the United Kingdom, and a person did not have to be a resident of Canada to enjoy the privileges accorded to Canadian ships.
Before I resume my seat, Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize one point made by the hon. member for Gloucester. Since we are amending the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act, and since these amendments are so very rare and infrequent, it is a pity that the government did not see fit to include in this bill some clarification of our territorial waters; because this bill applies to territorial waters, and I do not think we can dissociate our discussion of this bill from some discussion of the territorial waters to which it applies. When I looked up the debate in 1952, when the last amendment was made, I noted that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, now the Acting Prime Minister, who was then the member for Vancouver Quadra, pointed out two things; first that in the main act as we have it today the definition of our territorial waters is not clear. He asked for a clarification of that point.
The second point made was that our territorial waters should be extended. I believe it was said at the time, that this question was being considered by an interdepartmental committee. I think it is safe to assume that departmental committee has finished its work and has made some recommendations in this matter. It would have been helpful if the minister had included those recommendations in this bill we now have before us. I refer particularly to the definition of coastal waters. It is not clear to many people whether we determine our coastal waters on a point to point basis, that is on a straight line from headland to headland, or just by following the contour of the coast and extending it three miles offshore. The minister will appreciate the fact that this particular bill will not contribute very much to the solution of the problem of protecting the coastal fisheries in my own particular riding because our best inshore fishing grounds are 12 miles offshore. Unless we can control our coastal waters to that extent our inshore fishermen will always be deprived of the opportunity of earning a livelihood because of foreign drag-gers fishing in this area.

subtopic: REVISION OF DEFINITION OF CANADIAN FISHING VESSEL

subtopic: REVISION OF DEFINITION OF CANADIAN FISHING VESSEL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it would be a grave mistake to narrow too much the right of an individual to own a Canadian vessel. Problems could arise if a man had to be both domiciled and resident in Canada and had to be able to swear he was a Canadian citizen. I think of people associated with some of our fish plants in the east. They would have to be prepared to swear that they intended permanently to live here. They may not in fact do so, but they must state theii intention to do so in order to qualify as a person domiciled in Canada.
What would be done in effect by changing the wording to specify a domiciled resident of Canada would be to rule out from the definition a United States citizen who happened to be transferred to Canada as manager of, or executive of a fish plant and who might be here five or ten years but who would perhaps eventually go back home to Boston or wherever the head office of the plant may be.
I think it would be a mistake to adopt the wording suggested, and I should like to see the minister further examine the legal meaning of this language before a change is made in the clause. I think it would be a serious mistake to say we should limit the ownership of Canadian vessels to Canadian citizens actually living in Canada.
The situation is not unknown in my riding, and some other ridings on the east coast, where a man associated with some of the fish plants owned in the United States moves back and forth between the maritime or Atlantic area of Canada and the New England area of the United States. If we limit the ownership under the definition to a person who is a Canadian citizen actually resident and domiciled in Canada we would, under this narrow definition, eliminate many people who now own vessels or who may in the future be encouraged to operate vessels out of Canadian Atlantic ports.

subtopic: REVISION OF DEFINITION OF CANADIAN FISHING VESSEL
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member a question before he resumes his seat. I do not wish to be overly critical but the draftsmanship of this particular bill is rather strange and could lead to a variety of conclusions. I understand one of the rules of draftsmanship is that you use the same words throughout a statute if they are to mean the same thing. In lines 9 and 10 reference is made to ownership by one or more persons. In this instance persons are referred to. In line 11 we no longer refer to persons but to individuals. We draw some distinction between an individual and a person. Is one person who owns a fishing vessel and is a Canadian citizen different from an individual who is a Canadian citizen and who also owns a fishing vessel? For the sake of clarity, it seems to me that the word "person" should be used throughout so that we would know what we are talking about.
I make reference to this part of the act only for this specific purpose. Subsection 3 of section 3 of the act makes reference to person. It says "no person". In other parts of the act, reference is made to persons. For instance, the section on offences and penalties says that every person is guilty of an offence who does certain things. Section 8 says, "Every person who violates" and so on. Throughout there is reference to the word "person" either in its singular or plural form. It would seem to me that the word "individual" is sort of out of place if we mean the same thing as we mean when we use the word "person". It would seem to me that we should be consistent throughout and use the word "person" in place of "individual". The amendment reads in part:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

Do you not feel, therefore, that you should reserve the right to make a decision on these technical problems? Do you think that you, as a member of parliament, are qualified to pass judgment on this?

I do not think I am qualified to pass on the technical aspects. However, I took an interest in this; I went to the hearings before the Senate, and I was here during the hearings on the Foothills bill. I am not speaking with any expert knowledge, but I say I think it is my right as a member of parliament, when this comes before us, to pass my judgment and to object.
Then the hon. member for Calgary South said:
You think it is your right, but you have said you do not think you are qualified.

That is right.
Then the hon. member for Bow River said:
Actually you said you do not like to hand over that jurisdiction; but did you not, as a fact, when you voted for the national energy board, actually hand over that authority to the national energy board?
I quote that passage to indicate the implications behind the remarks that this is a matter that should not seriously concern parliament, that it is to a greater extent the responsibility of the national energy board. As against that point of view I wish to quote briefly from the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East. On page 39 the hon. member is reported as having said:

The only matters which come before the national energy board are those authorized by parliament. It would depend on whether or not the company is incorporated. That is what we are
discussing now.
I quote that passage to indicate the contrast between the point of view of the hon. members we oppose in this connection and of this group. The hon. member for Vancouver East was reflecting our approach as socialists. This questioning as reported in the minutes of the committee clearly indicates our great concern for the rights, responsibilities and the institution of parliament.
We in this group consider that this bill, in essence, conflicts with stated government policy. In the speech from the throne to the Canadian parliament on November 17, 1960, announcements were made regarding one of the most important subjects dealt with in

Private Bills
a report, to which I intend to refer. I wish to quote from the speech from the throne:
You will be invited to consider means by which to encourage a greater participation by Canadians in the ownership and control of industry and resources in Canada.
That is one of the main arguments of this group. We say this bill does not give effect to government policy which has been stated. Only one member on the government side emphasized that point of view and supported our point of view. It is very interesting to see the Conservative party split on this issue, and I think it will split wider and wider as we approach election day. However, at least one member agreed with us. The hon. member for Medicine Hat is generally so good-natured that what he said was rather unusual.

How did you
stand on Northern Pipe Line?
The way I always stand, straight up.
What is the difference?

I hope I will not be interrupted for the few minutes longer that I wish to speak. I wish to quote from a report entitled "Policies and Practices of United States Subsidiaries in Canada" issued by the Canadian-American Committee. I may say that this committee is sponsored by the national planning association of the United States and by the private planning association of Canada, and it has been dealing with the very kind of question involving United States capital investment as we are concerned about it in this present bill. The main body of the study deals with major aspects of the behaviour of United States subsidiaries in Canada, including the issue of equity security by subsidiaries; personnel policies; the publication of financial reports and other information; commercial policy; research activities, and contributions to charity and education.
A great deal of information is brought out in this booklet and I am not going to quote from it at any length now, but the report provides a very sound basis for argument in opposition to legislation of the type now before us. I should like to quote from page 10 of this report:
It has been amply demonstrated that successful modern management usually subordinates the immediate and narrow interest of its stockholders to the long term interest of the corporation. Especially where foreign operations are involved, this often calls for conscious effort to fall in line with the aspirations of the community in which the enterprise operates even if it involves substantial policy changes which are not of apparent immediate advantage to the present corporation as a whole.

Elsewhere, the report states:
There is also the pressure which comes from the obligation of management to operate its business, wherever located, in the broad interest of its stockholders.
That is what we must expect with regard to the operations of this particular company in the days to come. Further on in this report, the conclusion is reached:
In certain respects the criticism which some Canadians-including some in high places-make of United States business firms in Canada is unreasonable.
That is fair enough.
Often it involves sweeping generalizations based on the alleged actions of a few companies. Sometimes it calls for policy changes which it would be unrealistic to expect from any business, whether owned and run by Canadians, Americans, or anyone else.
We are not asking for something which is unrealistic but we are asking that consideration be given to Canadian ownership, Canadian directors, and policies which are in conformity with local and national interests when we are considering the incorporation of these pipe line companies. I should like to put on record one final quotation from page 80 of this booklet:
That this demand for Canadianization is growing has become apparent during the course of this study. Well informed Canadians see this as taking the form of pressure for legislation affecting such things as foreign equity ownership, Canadianization of directorships, and the publication of financial and other data. Many Canadians, who are accustomed to reform through persuasion and accommodation, look upon the possibility of such legislation with misgiving. In this they reflect the concern of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects that under some conditions the Canadian reaction to extensive foreign ownership and control "might develop into demands for restrictive or discriminatory action of an extreme kind, the consequences of which would be unfortunate for all concerned."
This report will have served its purpose if, as was said in the opening chapter, it adds greater understanding on the Canadian side of the actual policies and practices, and the reasons for them, of a good cross section of United States controlled companies in Canada, and if on the American side it gives to some parent companies a greater appreciation of the importance to Canadians of their own national aspirations.
We wish to be fair. We do not expect the impossible. We recognize the circumstances under which these companies are financed, controlled and operated. However, we in this group feel there is a principle at stake, and we have to fight for the greater consideration of the national and local interest with regard to the incorporation of this company.
So, in concluding my brief remarks, I wish to say that we oppose this bill because we think it is wrong in principle for the reasons which I and other members of this group have put forward. Another reason is that we believe insufficient study was given in committee to

the proposals in this legislation. That is obvious when one considers the importance of the bill and compares that with the slenderness of the report itself. One has only to bear in mind the repeated additions to the information received from the hon. member for Bow River as the debate has proceeded; as day follows day, another leaf is turned in the hon. member's book of information, and its contents made available to hon. members of this committee. All that information could have been presented to the committee when it was studying this bill. We were given to understand that when the bill had received second reading there would be an exhaustive, extensive and intensive study undertaken in the committee.
The second reason for our opposition to the bill is, thus, because of the fact that inadequate study was given to this question by the committee. Finally, we do not believe that legislation of this type is, in the long run, in the national or the provincial or the local interest.

I intend to be brief. I should like to take advantage of the offer made by the hon. member for Bow River when he said, as reported on page 2936 of Hansard of March 13:
If there are any points which any hon. member conscientiously and honestly believes have been left unexplained, will he put the question in a few words, and I for my part, will try to give an answer in a few words?
I have three questions to ask the hon. member for Bow River. First, in regard to the 12,000 public stockholders referred to by Mr. Burgis, how many of those stockholders are Canadians or residents in Canada, and what percentage of the total stock distributed of Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas do they own? Second, of the personnel, the operating management-the entire personnel-of Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company, how many aliens are employed in the operation?
The hon. member has already answered the question. I put to him with regard to the construction work, although 1 wonder how the story was so common around Calgary. However, I accept the hon. member's word and the statement made by the company that they intend to use Canadian contractors. Incidentally, I have a great deal of sympathy for the hon. member for Bow River because he is having a rough time. I had a similar experience a couple of years back when I piloted the bill through for the incorporation of the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company. I fought tooth and nail with hon. members over in the corner, but finally they saw reason and the bill went through. However, it was not until the second year that it did.
Private Bills
My third question is this: is the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company planning to increase the percentage of Canadian participation either through the issuance of treasury stock along the line followed by the Alberta Natural Gas Company or other issues recently made in Canada which have been limited to participation by Canadians, if Canadians wanted to buy? In other words, is this company going to become more Canadian?
Now I want to take exception to a remark made by the hon. member for Assiniboia. As reported on page 2930 of Hansard for March 13 the hon. member spoke as follows:
I would suggest that it is little wonder, because of all the bad features of this bill, that the members of the government party on the committee voted against the motion merely to defer consideration of the bill in the committee so that interested witnesses might have the opportunity to appear.
It is only fair to say that the mover of that motion was the hon. member for Westmorland and the seconder was a member of Her Majesty's Privy Council for Canada, the dean of the house, and they certainly are Conservatives. The person who moved the motion that the committee should recess until a reporter appeared to take evidence was not an alive and alert member of the C.C.F. but the hon. member for the Yukon, although the hon. member for Skeena did second that motion.
I think that hon. members should be fair about this and recognize that the hon. members from Alberta have a problem. I can sympathize with them. The development of the oil and gas industries in Alberta is vital. At this time it has been decided that there are far-reaching national considerations which must be examined in the development of national resources. The purpose is not to stop that development but to give it a pattern. That has been the theme of what I have said in this committee and in the house on second reading.
It is only right and just that the people who come here to assist in the development of national resources should make a profit. The development of our natural resources is a profitable business. It is just and fair that they make their operations good for themselves and for Canada. These are not incompatible statements. This is not Saudi Arabia where the government takes 50 per cent of the royalty, and I believe is now negotiating for 60 per cent or 75 per cent. In Alberta the royalty is 12J per cent. This royalty is valuable to the people and the government of Alberta. It is a reasonable royalty.
The conditions which have been set out and embodied in the Natural Energy Board Act are reasonable. The thought behind that

Private Bills
act is reasonable. The way the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources is handling the development of oil and gas resources in the Arctic is in line with that act, and with the philosophy about which I have been speaking. That philosophy is reflected in the form of certain public bills I have placed on the order paper. There is a coherence and an underlying thread all the way through that we shall not discriminate against foreign capital but shall welcome it,, provided it works in partnership with Canadian capital.
In closing my remarks at this stage let me say this to my hon. friends from Alberta. Seventy or eighty thousand United States citizens may run the gas and oil industry in Alberta, but I suggest that Alberta is growing to the point where Albertans can operate many of these enterprises and surely the people of Canada can now participate in every phase of these operations.
Let us have a little bit of sense and reason in this debate. Let us take out the wild statements, such as those made by the hon. member for Assiniboia and those made by the hon. member for Kootenay West when he spoke about the Conservative split. There is no split in the Conservative party. The policy of our party has not changed.
We are discussing a private bill. All hon. members have the right to say what they think in this respect, but I do not think any hon. member or any group has the right to hold up passage of a bill. Hon. members have the right to dissent, but not to obstruct. We can make our positions known when the time comes for the taking of a vote.
When will that be?

I trust I shall not be the only hon. member on this side of the committee who will vote against this bill on third reading, but that is my intention unless the hon. member for Bow River can satisfy me in respect of the three questions I have put to him. This is my last word in this debate at the committee stage.
Mr. Chairman, perhaps if the hon. member for Bow River cares to answer the questions put to him by the hon. member for Vancouver South my remarks might be somewhat curtailed.
That would be a good thing.
In view of the fact that the hon. member does not care to answer or has no answers to the questions posed by the hon. member for Vancouver South I have no choice but to proceed with my-[DOT]
Filibuster?

-remarks in the ordinary course. I have listened carefully

to the debate and followed it closely in Hansard. I must admit my knowledge of the oil and gas industry is not too wide and that is why I listened with such interest to the discussion.
I am interested in this bill and in bills of this nature. My riding is, as it were, at the other end of the oil industry and my area, along with others, has supplied the gold with which this pipe line is apparently going to be plated.
This bill represents another in that series of sorry events that have occurred relating to the development of our natural resources. History shows that in the main it has been a question of development of those resources by quick-buck artists. What makes the present bill even more odious is the fact that the quick-buck artists involved are not even of the home-grown variety.
The hon. member for Timiskaming referred last evening to the decline and virtual disappearance of the white pine industry. This came about because of the methods employed by the quick buck artists in the development of our resources. Another recent example is found in the uranium industry. Under a five-year contract the Rio Tinto company took out $93 million net, and those who got it in the neck were individuals who were unfortunate enough to have purchased homes in the area of that industry.
This quick-buck artistry has never been better illustrated than in the development of our oil industry. A most glaring example was the trans-Canada pipe line fiasco of a couple of years ago which resulted in bringing the Liberal government crashing down to earth. Another example recently exposed was that of a western oil company which proceeded to dispose of its products in the United States at prices cheaper than those which were charged Canadian consumers along the route of the pipe line. Gas and oil should be available at cheap prices to Canadian but people have had to sell their homes because they could not keep up with the high cost of this great natural resource when used as fuel.
Because of this type of development, the benefit of this resource has been denied to our people. The costs of promotion have to be paid by someone and it is the consumer who pays. It may be that the costs are extended over so long a period that you will not have a chance in your lifetime to pay them, but will pass them on to your children and theirs. These paper profits are not supposed to hurt anyone but they do hurt the consumer and are built-in over a long period of time.
There have been interesting developments in this debate. The Liberals have been consistent in the position they took in 1956 of selling out Canadian interests to the United

States. I do not know if one should congratulate them for their consistency. Apparently they are prepared to follow the same consistent line in their approach to this pipe line company. We also see that the hon. member for Vancouver South was consistent with Conservative policy back in 1956, which was that quick-buck artistry is not too bad provided it is Canadian or, at least, if we are to have some quick-buck artistry it should be confined to Canadians. We should not sell out to United States interests.
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver South on his courage and forthrightness. His stand is consistent with what he believes to be the present Tory policy. An illustration of this is found in the excellent words which the hon. member used the other night, as reported at page 2680 of Hansard:
The only thing tor which this government has stood... is that Canadians can compete on equal terms with capital coming into this country from other sources.
Unfortunately, apparently this stand, which had been expounded so well by the hon. member for Vancouver South is not shared in this instance by the hon. member for Bow River, and certainly, at least during this debate, not by the two hornets from Acadia and Jasper-Edson. Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, I do not really believe the three hon. members have given a good reason for their stand, unless they are trying to do something which is going to benefit their particular ridings regardless of whether it is in the interests of the province as a whole. Certainly they seem to be disregarding the interests of Canadians as a whole.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

The hon. member spoke about benefiting a particular riding. I would ask him if Pincher Creek is in the riding of Bow River? From my knowledge of Alberta and western Canada, Pincher Creek is strictly within the riding of Macleod and has nothing to do with the riding of Bow River.

Mr. Chairman, possibly I did misrepresent the hon. member. If that was not the reason, then unfortunately there is another reason that I can see. We understand that the hon. member, contrary to Conservative policy past or present, appears to be acting in line with Social Credit policy during the pipe line debate of 1956.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman-

Our new Beauchesne.
Private Bills

Well, you need one. The hon. member for Timmins is attempting to develop a political case for the export of gas and oil, and he has cast some aspersions on the Alberta members. He has tried to talk about uranium, about which he knows very little, apparently; I have not seen him in the research committee.
There is no point of order.

Yes, there is. The point is simply that this debate is supposed to be about a bill having to do with a pipe line, not about Social Credit or the C.C.F. in Alberta, not about the personal views of Alberta members on a selfish basis. It was intimated a moment ago that we came from Alberta. We do, and we are proud of it and we are just as good Canadians as those who come from Ontario.

Mr. Chairman, certainly I do not think there is any accusation against an hon. member for saying that he is trying to do something for his particular riding. It may not be in the interests of the country as a whole, but I certainly do not think it is any reflection on any hon. member to say that he is trying to promote the interests of his own riding. I definitely try to promote the interests of my riding.
You are doing a damn poor job, then.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I do not think anybody is going to worry about your judgment on this matter or on any other matter.
He is out of order again.
If the hon. member thinks I am doing a bad job, I should like to invite him to debate that question in my riding.
He will probably take it out of Hansard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

There is another point I should like to illustrate; I think it is very important in so far as this particular bill is concerned. I should like to refer to the words of the Minister of Agriculture, formerly minister of northern affairs and national resources. I think the best illustration I can give is to quote just a few extracts from a speech made by the Minister of Agriculture in committee of supply when the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources were under discussion. His remarks were related to conservation and the development of our natural

Coastal Fisheries Protection Act resources. They certainly are apropos of this particular bill. This is what the minister had to say:
-we are the nation on the northern half of this continent and we want to make certain that the interests, not only of the present generation, are protected, but that the interests of generations unborn will also be preserved.
I should like to ask the hon. member for Bow River whether a bill of this kind, when practically all the control of the company is outside of our country, can be construed as applying to the policy expressed by the Minister of Agriculture?

Will the hon. member permit a question? On this matter of outside control, I think it would be of interest to the committee, since the members of the C.C.F. party are filibustering this bill, if the hon. member would tell us what percentage of United States capital is invested in the exploitation of gas and oil in Saskatchewan?
I would love to debate that particular issue with the hon. member at some time but I do not think we can do so now.
I should like to inform the hon. member that over 75 per cent is United States capital. If the hon. member continues to filibuster this bill I do not see how we can waste our time listening to him.

Wrong again.
Progress reported.

subtopic: FARM MACHINERY PRICES

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (for the Minister of Agriculture) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: FARM MACHINERY PRICES
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF INQUIRY BY STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: That the standing committee on agriculture and colonization be empowered to continue its inquiry into the question of prices of farm machinery as recommended by the said committee in its fourth report presented to the house July 28, 1960, and that the committee's minutes of proceedings and evidence with regard to this inquiry at the last session be referred to the said committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. H. Jorgenson (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: FARM MACHINERY PRICES
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF INQUIRY BY STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am
sure that all hon. members are aware of the widespread interest in this question of farm machinery prices. No member representing a rural constituency could possibly avoid hearing the discussion of this subject. Farmers realize the necessity of keeping production costs down to a minimum in order to compete not only in the export market but in their own domestic market, and have expressed their concern regarding the rise in the price of farm machinery since 1955. The increase in production efficiency on the part of farmers is invariably lost because of the high cost of farm machinery.

On Monday, June 6, 1960, the house ordered that the standing committee on agriculture and colonization be empowered to inquire into the prices of farm machinery and to report to the house thereon. The committee held three open meetings and the persons appearing before the committee at the last session were as follows: Mr. A. D. Holmes, Director, Prices Division, Dominion Bureau of Statistics; Mr. R. A. Stutt and Mr. G. Haase, Department of Agriculture; Messrs. D. W. McGill, Director, and J. J. A. Lefebvre, Machinery Section Head, Appraisers Branch, Department of National Revenue; and Mr. J. T. Wimble of the Appraisers Branch, National Revenue and Mr. W. Kalbfleisch, Chief of the Engineering Research Service, Department of Agriculture.
The chairman gave the following report to the house on Thursday, July 28, which reads as follows:
Your committee has noted the wide-spread interest in the subject of farm machinery prices.
Your committee held four meetings on this order of reference. It heard representatives from the dominion bureau of statistics on farm machinery prices; from the Department of National Revenue on farm machinery tariffs; from the engineering research service of the Department of Agriculture on the different types of farm machinery.
Your committee has found that interested persons or organizations would like more time to prepare presentations.
Your committee recommends;
1.	That the subject of farm machinery prices be referred to it as soon as possible after the opening of the next session of parliament.
2.	That the ministers of the different government departments concerned, instruct their officers to offer every assistance to the persons designated by the committee to procure and compile all available facts regarding farm machinery prices.
During the recess a summary of statistics relative to the inquiry into the price of farm machinery, under the direction of Mr. Gordon Haase of the economics division of the Department of Agriculture, has been prepared. Copies of this report will be made available to the members of the committee both in English and in French as soon as possible, when the committee is prepared to resume its investigation.
No one at this time is prepared to say just where the responsibility lies for the price increase. It is to be hoped that during committee sessions an investigation in this regard will take place following which recommendations will be made as to how to minimize the present increase and prevent any further increase.
I do not think it is necessary for me to indicate the nature of the inquiry which should take place, but I am sure that the committee
Farm. Machinery Prices will investigate that which they may deem necessary, whether it be in the manufacturing, distribution or retail field.
I might also add that the interest in all phases of the industry has been shown by the people concerned. It is expected that their views will be heard, in addition to the representations by labour and agriculture. I hope that this motion will be passed today and that the committee will be able to resume its inquiry at the earliest possible opportunity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we welcome the statement just made by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Jorgenson). I want to assure him that we welcome this opportunity of looking again into this matter, because we believe that this study is necessary on account of the questions that are being asked by many farmers and all those concerned with every aspect of agriculture.
It is the utmost importance, in our opinion, that the committee be once more authorized to continue its inquiry into the question of farm machinery prices; besides, the committee included such a recommendation in its fourth report to the house.
I shall speak very briefly tonight because I do not want to anticipate the results of the inquiry that will be conducted by the committee on agriculture and colonization.
This is not the first time, however, that we have been hearing about this committee and I should like to refer to the statement made by the former minister of agriculture on June 6, 1960, as reported on page 4571 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, during the past 10 years, the most frequently heard general complaint on the part of farmers has been over the cost price squeeze. This arises from the fact that during this period the prices received by farmers for their products either have not increased or have not increased in anything like the proportion of the increase in cost of the goods and services farmers have to purchase.
Nothing could be more to the point, Mr. Speaker, and if we refer to D.B.S. figures, for instance, we note that the price index of goods and services purchased by farmers reached 255.9 in 1957; 259.9 in 1958; 269.5 in 1959; 274.4 in 1960. Therefore, from 1957 to the end of 1960, we note a 14.5 increase in the price index of goods and services purchased by farmers.
If, on the other hand, we refer to the same statistics, we find that the retail price index of farm products for 1956, was 234.6 and that it was 234.7 for the first 11 months of 1960.

Farm Machinery Prices
So, in four years, from 1956 to 1960, the percentage increase of the retail price of farm products was only 0.01.
This inquiry is a must, no doubt, and we, in the committee will give it all our attention but that does not seem to be the main cause of the cost-price squeeze. There may be deeper causes that could warrant a more objective investigation. For instance, what about the farm product marketing organization in this country? Nothing has been done in that field, although our economists have been discussing the problem and have recommended a study of marketing methods by a research committee.
After the then minister of agriculture, on June 6, 1960, had instructed the committee on agriculture and colonization to inquire into farm machinery prices, we hoped that the committee would get to work immediately. But it was not until July 12 next that the first meeting was held. It was followed by three more, on July 19, 26 and 27, 1960. At those meetings, evidence was heard from officers of the departments of agriculture and national revenue, and also from the dominion bureau of statistics. And it was only at the last meeting that we were given questionnaires.
And I think that all the members of the committee had copies distributed to the farmers in their ridings in order to find out what they thought of this price margin on farm machinery.
In 1960, that is during the last session, the committee on agriculture and colonization had this to say in its fourth report:
(Text):
Your committee has found that interested persons or organizations would like more time to prepare presentations.
Your committee recommends:
1. That the subject of farm machinery prices be referred to it as soon as possible after the opening of the next session of parliament.
(Translation):
Who is to blame, Mr. Speaker, we do not know or perhaps we do know it only too well. Still, certain questions remain unanswered in our minds. We wonder what caused the Minister of Agriculture and the government to delay for four months this year the opening of the inquiry by the committee on agriculture and colonization. Even if we blamed the committee for not having met more often last year to consider this matter, I think we must once more blame the government and in stronger terms for this year's four months delay.
Does the government feel that this matter is not important? Does it think that the situation which the farmer must face, as far as


the purpose of this inquiry is concerned, is not important? We do not know. And I would not like to put words in the mouth of the minister. However, we cannot help wondering whether the delay suffered in this matter is not deliberate.
We are really wondering whether the new Minister of Agriculture considers what the situation will be at the time of the next general election when the farmers will remind him that the price spread still exists.
The minister might then tell the farmers that his government has foreseen this development and that an inquiry is in progress. Unfortunately, since this government came to power, we have too often seen similar electoral tactics whose only aim is to create a smokescreen to cover the true situation.
However, we on this side do wish that the committee on agriculture and colonization will make haste in order that a report may be submitted to the house before the end of the present session. That is what we hope for and, therefore, we wish the committee to be called as soon as possible.
In closing, I should like to tell the Minister of Agriculture, or, in the circumstances, his parliamentary secretary, that if it so happens that the committee is unable to examine fully this whole question this year, we on this side of the house would suggest that a commission be established to complete the inquiry.
May I repeat that the announcement by the parliamentary secretary of the establishment of this committee is most welcome. We on this side of the house who are members of the committee on agriculture and colonization assure him that we will fully co-operate in order to inform not only the house but in particular our farmers who will know at last what to believe in this matter.
