subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF INQUIRY BY STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the whole question of prices of agricultural machinery is an exceedingly important one as far as some 600,000 farm families in Canada are concerned. There is probably no item going into the farmer's cost of production that is larger, more necessary or causes him greater concern than the cost of agricultural equipment.
Farmers have faced many grave problems since the end of the war. One has been a failure to obtain markets for agricultural production. Another has been a failure to obtain relatively good prices for agricultural commodities, and a third and very important one has been the almost astronomical increase in the price of agricultural machinery.

According to the statistics which are available prices of agricultural machinery have increased by almost two and a half times since the beginning of world war II. Farm cash income since the end of the war has remained relatively stable, with a small percentage increase over that period of time. In the farmers' view agricultural machinery is a fixed cost over which he has no control, and it is a burden that is resting very heavily on the agricultural industry.
There is a move for expansion and consolidation of farms in Canada and there is tremendous pressure to force farm populations off the farms. I do not think any item has contributed more to the depopulation of agricultural areas than the impossible burden of agricultural machinery prices for most farmers. Since this is such an important matter one would have thought the government would have taken early action to do something about it.
We are dealing with this matter on March 14. It was first raised in the House of Commons on June 6, 1960, and a report was made to parliament by the agricultural committee on July 28, 1960. This report recommended that the subject of farm machinery prices be referred to that committee as soon as possible after the opening of the next session of parliament.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) has failed to carry out the recommendation of the committee. He has failed to bring this motion before the house at an early date in the session. Parliament opened on November 17. It is almost four months since this session began. It has taken the government four months to get this resolution on the order paper, even in the face of a recommendation from the agricultural committee that the question of farm machinery prices be referred to it as soon as possible after the opening of the next session of parliament.
I suggest that the government, by its procrastination and delay has been blocking its own inquiry and has been making it more difficult for the committee to bring forward recommendations at an early date. I suggest that the government, by these delaying tactics, has shown that its well-known promises to bring about a balance between prices of agricultural products and the cost of agricultural machinery have gone by the board and have been repudiated. I suggest that this committee may well provide a great deal of window-dressing and very little action.
The question of agricultural machinery prices is of tremendous importance because according to dominion bureau of statistics figures farmers spent just under $55 million on farm implements in 1944 and $251 million
Farm Machinery Prices in 1959. That is an increase of five times in the amount of money spent on agricultural machinery. Yet in the face of this tremendous problem and the urgency to do something about it the government has long delayed bringing forward this important motion.
I think there are many items which should be brought before the committee. I think we should bring witnesses before the committee from the main agricultural implement companies in this country. We should ask them to appear before the committee and explain, if they can, why they have done such a poor job in maintaining reasonable prices for agricultural machinery. This spells a difficult problem for Canada because most of the farm implement companies have their head offices located outside our country. It is a question of whether or not we can get witnesses from the majority of these companies- I hope we can, but it does present a problem-since their head offices are located outside this country.
A few years ago the legislature of Saskatchewan undertook an inquiry into the farm implement industry. The inquiry was held in 1952, I believe, and it was a rather exhaustive one. Witnesses from the various agricultural implement companies were asked to come before the committee. The farm implement companies, with the exception of Canadian Co-operative Implements Limited, boycotted the committee, refused to appear and therefore made the work of the committee very difficult.
I trust we will exercise our authority where possible, and our influence where our authority does not extend, to have the representatives of the main agricultural implement companies in Canada appear before our committee. I think we should have representatives from Canadian Co-operative Implements Limited, the Massey-Harris Company, which in substantial part is a Canadian company, and from Cockshutt Farm Equipment Limited, which is also a Canadian company. We should also request the attendance of witnesses from companies situated in the United States. I refer to such companies as the John Deere Company, the International Harvester Company, the Minneapolis Moline Company, the Case Company, the Oliver Company, and any others we think should appear before the committee.
There are a number of questions we should ask them. I think we should ask them why we have such a conglomeration of models with modifications in agricultural machinery. I think the farm implement industry is getting almost in the position of the automobile industry. Through an excessive advertising campaign the implement companies have been trying to sell streamlined tractors with special

Farm Machinery Prices gadgets. They are following the plans of the automobile companies in this regard, not with the objective of making durable implements that will last for a long period of time, but to bring forward farm implements that fall into the category of having been produced and distributed on the basis of planned obsolescence. Then within a few years, by large scale promotion they hope to again sell these implements to agricultural producers.
In addition to planned obsolescence, there is the question of the power content of many farm implements. I think the companies are promoting power in agricultural implements in exactly the same way as automobile companies have been promoting power in automobiles. I think there is a rather important question as to whether or not they have overdone the feature of power with, of course, a very large increase in cost.
I think there is another important question which the committee should study in its inquiry. I refer to the question of providing spare parts for repairing agricultural implements. It seems to me that farm implement companies do not keep on hand a stock of spare parts for a sufficient number of years. After a few years it is difficult to obtain parts for the implements that have been sold, and farmers must travel 50, 75 or 100 miles or more to a large centre in the hope that they can get repairs made. Even in my part of the country, if they travel to Regina they may be told: we shall have to send to Winnipeg, or we shall have to send to the factory. I think the companies have done a very poor job, a very inadequate job, with regard to providing a complete stock of spare parts likely to be required for their machines over the probable life of the farm implements. I think this is a question into which the committee should make a full inquiry.
I do not know why the government has set up the committee or why they are proposing this motion. They say-the parliamentary secretary has said-it is an endeavour to prevent farm implements costing more or, even better, that it is an endeavour to reduce the price of farm implements. These are certainly laudable objectives. But every time one asks the government to do something about the way in which the great corporations of this country are operated, every time you ask them to plan production or to control prices, what does the government say? It says: we cannot touch free enterprise; it is beyond our control and beyond our jurisdiction. So I would be anxious to learn from the parliamentary secretary just in what way this government feels it can exercise any control over the farm implement companies of this country. I suggest that the government has abandoned responsibility with regard to the


operation of these companies, because the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has told us very often that the government has no authority over private business and its operations. When we ask in this house whether or not, for example, General Motors is going to close down a plant in Windsor, the answer is: we have no control; it is beyond our jurisdiction. Very often the government will not even go as far as to make inquiries. If the government takes the attitude that it has no control over the auto industry, how does it expect to bring about the laudable objectives mentioned in connection with this particular committee?
There is the question of price spread, the difference between manufacturing costs and retail cost. There is the great problem of the price spread in the food industry. We had a royal commission set up under this government which brought in a report, but instead of price spreads being narrowed they continued to increase. One can only wonder whether there is a conscientious endeavour on the part of this government to bring about some revision in farm implement prices or whether this is just another case of window dressing, a case of holding a talk-fest and doing nothing about the problem. We have, I think, in Canada an oportunity to do something about farm implement prices because, unlike certain other countries we do have a native farm implement industry. We have the Massey-Harris Company, the Cockshutt Company and Canadian Co-Operative Implements Limited. I suggest that this committee should consider the financial support and encouragement of the co-operative production of farm implements and there should be a full inquiry as to whether we should use to a much greater extent the facilities of CoOperative Implements Limited so as to bring about a reduction in prices. I think we should consider the possibility of public ownership in the field of farm implements.

I am pointing out some of the problems in the farm implement industry, some of the things into which I think inquiry should be made. I think the whole question of the kind of production we should have in the farm implement field is certainly an area into which the committee should make inquiry.
There is another area in which I think the committee should make inquiry. I would ask the parliamentary secretary if it is the intention that the inquiry should proceed along these lines, namely, an investigation into the costs of the various components

which make up the prices of farm implements such as the cost of salaries, wages, overhead, profits and materials. I should like to see appearing before this committee not only experts from the farm implement industry but experts from labour and management to put before the committee information as to the various component costs going into the price of farm implements.
I have in my hand a survey which has been made relating to these costs. This survey is contained in a publication put out by the farm-labour co-ordinating council, which is a body composed of representatives of labour, the Canadian Labour Congress and its affiliated unions, and representatives of the farm unions of Canada. This body found that, comparing 1957 costs with 1945 costs, there has been an increase of 8 per cent in the cost of salaries, an increase of 7.5 per cent in overhead and profits, a reduction in the cost of fuel and electricity by .4 per cent, an increase in the costs of material by 3.1 per cent and a reduction in the cost of labour amounting to 11 per cent. In 1957, wages accounted for 22.9 per cent of the final price of farm implements as compared with 33.9 per cent in 1945.
The bogey has been raised that the higher prices of farm machinery can be attributed to higher labour costs. Let us find out if this accusation can be substantiated. According to this source of information, that is not the case. Increased efficiency and automation have resulted in the reduction of the percentage of cost attributable to labour, and there has been a substantial increase in such things as overhead, profits, salaries and materials.
We trust that the committee will do something about reducing farm implement prices and that it will not be just another talk-fest, another inquiry bringing in another report to gather dust while farm machinery prices continue to rise.

I shall be glad to answer any question which the hon. member wishes to raise after I have finished my remarks. Let hon. gentlemen in that corner be quiet and take their medicine.
Neither hon. members of the house from agricultural constituencies nor the farmers of western Canada have to be told by the hon. member for Assiniboia that farm costs are one of the most important problems facing the agricultural economy. It is a well-known fact that the price of farm machinery weighs heavily on western Canadian farmers.
The net income position of farmers is determined by two factors, costs on the one hand and prices for commodities on the other. These two factors operate like the two blades of a pair of scissors, and one cannot tell which is doing the most cutting in so far as net income is concerned.
At this time the government is embarking on a study relating to the cost side of the picture. Through the work of this committee the government is seeking to assess the problems relative to the costs of machinery as

Farm Machinery Prices they affect the agricultural producers of western Canada. Economists have been working on many aspects of the problem for the past six months and I understand a wealth of material has been prepared relative thereto. It is also my understanding that representatives of the farm machinery companies and others will be called before the committee to give evidence. Therefore I say that the work that is about to be undertaken by this standing committee should lead to results and produce information which the farmers of western Canada are eagerly awaiting.
I, too, feel a little disturbed about the fact that the committee did not proceed sooner. At the same time, I realized that the delay was in large part due to the death of the hon. gentleman who served as chairman of the committee. Mr. Stanton put a tremendous effort into the work of the committee. He laid the groundwork for this price study and engaged in extensive correspondence in connection therewith. Had Mr. Stanton lived and continued in good health, I am sure this committee would have been functioning months ago.
In all fairness to the government, it should be said that the work that is about to be undertaken by the standing committee deserves the support and assistance of all hon. members of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all the members of the house will agree with the parliamentary secretary and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) that the motion before us tonight is a very good one indeed.
Many members have already spoken here on the price spread between the cost of farm implements and their sales price. Farmers in my area had brought up the matter and I raised the matter in the house last year.
The leader of the C.C.F. party said a moment ago that over 600,000 Canadian families are involved here. The cost of farm production has obviously been an important factor in farm desertion not only in Canada, not only in the other nine Canadian provinces should I say, but also in the province of Quebec.
The government was therefore will advised to request the committee on agriculture and colonization to investigate the reasons for such a price spread. Above all, I hope the committee will make useful recommendations for the government to implement in due course.

Last year, during the debate on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, more precisely on May 6, 1960, on behalf of many people who had brought the matter to my attention, I asked the government to create a royal commission to study this price spread. Exactly a month later, on June 6, the minister announced that the committee would deal with that situation.
I am prepared to congratulate the committee if it is in a position to accomplish as useful a task as would a royal commission. However I question this, not because of inability on the part of any members of the committee, but mainly because the standing committee on agriculture and colonization has many other subjects to consider and to look fully into.
It seems to me that, had a royal commission been appointed for the sole purpose of dealing with this particular matter, the government would have benefitted from very specific recommendations on the causes of this price spread and on the ways and means to prevent another increase and especially, on the ways and means to reduce the cost-price squeeze.
I fully agree with the member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue) that the committee should summon representatives of large manufacturers of farm machinery in this country. So far the committee has taken evidence only from officials of certain government departments.
I hope it will not be long before representatives of those large industries are summoned to answer certain questions put by the committee.
However, that is all the admiration I have for the solutions suggested or promoted by the hon. member for Assiniboia.
My hon. colleague even suggested that the government nationalize the large concerns selling farm machinery in Canada. Although I am very definitely in favour of private enterprise, I also believe that the government must intervene where private enterprise is detrimental to some sectors of our economy. But between that and nationalizing it, there is quite a margin.
I no longer believe in paradise on earth, Mr. Speaker, nor in incarnate purity in human beings. What distinguishes us is not purity, but veraying degrees of impurity.
People try to have us believe that those new messiahs and prophets will put an end to human misery. I would only ask the government to see to it that the committee

gather useful information, in order to abolish that spread between the production cost and selling price of farm machinery.
No need to go any further than the information gathered by the Stewart commission on price spreads for agricultural products, where it was shown that, in certain cases, two or three large companies in this country were making net profits of up to 33J per cent, after operation costs and taxes. I think there is an abuse there on the part of private enterprise. I do not want to have private enterprise eliminated, when it does its duty for the greater welfare of this country, but I do want the government to intervene and put a stop to such abuses.
I trust that the standing committee on agriculture and colonization will stand up to its responsibilities, as the other committees of the house do, and I more particularly wish to see some concrete proposals made to this government which would contribute to eliminate that spread which is conducive to the desertion of the land.
If it is impossible to gather all the information needed to put a stop to such conditions, I hope that the Minister of Agriculture will see to it that a royal commission is appointed without delay in which will be vested all necessary powers enabling it to draw conclusions which will help the government introduce legislation to put an end to such state of affairs in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak for a few moments in support of this motion to set up a committee to study the cost of agricultural machinery. You know, Mr. Speaker, I represent a different generation of farmers from those represented by the hon. member for Assini-boia. I represent a generation that lived under different conditions and experienced circumstances that he never experienced. I also represent a different type of farmer. Circumstances have changed a great deal in 55 years, Mr. Speaker.
I am reminded of the great change of circumstances when I think of the day we first stepped off a river steamer on a beach facing a mountain forest. I think of all the machinery we had. We first had to put off the steamer our settlers' effects which were on the bow of the steamer. First was my father's silk top hat in a leather case, and the second group of articles included an axe, a cross-cut saw, a shovel, a grubhoe and a crowbar. I shall never forget my father turning to my mother, pointing to the top hat and saying, "Charlotte, behold the symbol of the leisured past", and then pointing to this assembled group of pioneer farm machinery, all our machinery at that time, and saying,
Farm Machinery Prices "Behold, the symbol of the damned uncertain future".
After listening to the hon. member for Assiniboia tonight I must say it seems to me that the price of farm machinery is still the symbol of the damned uncertain future so far as our farmers are concerned, anyway.
There have been great changes from when I was a boy. I said I represent a different type of farmer. I represent farmers who at one time did most of their work by hand. Some of them had one horse and some had two. When you had two horses you were wealthy. They cut their roots for the cattle with an axe or spade and cut their hay with a scythe. I mention these things to indicate the tremendous changes that have taken place when we hear about the cost of the gigantic prairie machines.
I represent farmers who have, relatively speaking in relation to prairie farmers, small holdings; some stock farmers, those with the larger holdings, some poultry farmers,_ dairy farmers, a good many fruit farmers and some mink farmers. They use a different type of machinery. To some extent they have tractors, spraying machines and all the things required to do this different type of work, different types of machines because of the nature of the terrain and type of farming.
No doubt, the cost of machinery has become an increasing problem, and possibly more so than on the larger acreages where the capital invested in machinery is usually smaller in proportion to the capital invested in land and buildings.
However, I was at a farmer's place in my constituency just before I came down to Ottawa. He was a friend of mine. I asked him what was the cost of the machinery he had on his farm. It was all paid for. He was not a man to buy on time at all. He had $40,000 worth of machinery on his small farm. In those circumstances such a thing would have been unheard of 25 or 30 years ago. Therefore, it is a serious problem; machinery is a serious cost factor with respect to the operations of all types of farming. I am very pleased to see this question is going to be given consideration by the committee. I do hope that the farm organizations will be heard, and representatives of the machinery companies and of labour organizations, so that the committee will get as complete a picture as possible. Because of the, shall I say, multitude of designs and types which, as the hon. member for Assiniboia mentioned increases unnecessarily the cost of farm machinery, I suggest that possibly the committee should hear from agricultural engineers, or persons connected with the design of farm machinery, to get their

Farm Machinery Prices ideas and see whether they could make some recommendation with respect to standardizing the design of various types of agricultural machinery that are required today.
Another thing the committee should go into is the question of distribution, the location of agencies, the cost of distribution, which I think in some cases is excessive because of the duplication of agents. That could be reduced possibly by some, shall I say, more scientific form of distribution, more scientific system of agencies and arrangements for the sale of farm machinery.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I wish to suggest that in the country in which I live there are a good many farmers, fruit farmers for instance, who make quite a substantial portion of their living off small fruit holdings, peach growing, cherry growing, apple growing, plum growing, pear growing, and such small fruits. I see the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) looking at me. He knows the sort of people about whom I am speaking. In addition they undertake parttime logging and, in some cases, small sawmill operations, practising a combination of agriculture and forestry. With respect to the people in my district, I suggest-

Mr. Speaker, as vice chairman of this committee I think I would be remiss if I did not comment briefly on this proposed measure. I would certainly be lacking in my duty if I allowed certain statements made by the hon. member for Assiniboia to stand without comment or contradiction. I can assure hon. members that we have solicited representations from various manufacturing firms regarding farm machinery, including the John Deere Company, International Harvester and Massey-Harris. I think we have had replies from all of them, and these replies have been brought to the attention of this committee. There has been a very sincere effort on the part of the government members of this committee to present the viewpoints of all concerned regarding the prices of farm machinery. We are very fortunate, both in the committee and this house, in having full representation from farm constituencies.
I might say that on April 23, 1959, as reported at page 2985 of Hansard, I brought the increase in the cost of farm machinery to the attention of this house. In the same year, as reported at page 2991 of Hansard, the hon. member for Bow River gave a detailed list of machinery prices and the increase which had taken place over a period of ten years. I think that all hon. members will appreciate the sincere effort of those members from farming constituencies in trying to find a solution to the problem of the increased cost of farm machinery.
I have in my hand, a small sprocket from a Massey-Harris swather which costs $9.35 and weighs only 14 ounces. This will give hon. members an indication of our feeling

that it is necessary to find a solution to the problems involved in the increasing cost of farm machinery.
I will not take up any more time at this stage, but I hope that this matter will be referred to the committee at this time.

I should like to say a word or two regarding the remarks made by previous speakers. I was especially interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). I imagine all members of this house will agree that when his father got off the boat and looked at his tools and implements, he regarded himself as a capitalist because he probably owned them. One of the problems facing today's farmer, because of the high cost of these farming implements, is the financing of the necessary equipment to carry out his farm operations. Many farmers in Canada will never own their own machinery but will, as in the case of individuals purchasing automobiles and trucks, be continually financing new models.
The needle referred to by the hon. member for MacLeod (Mr. Kindt) must have indeed been sharp because it produced a number of squawks from that member. I think he was very unfair in his reference to the delay in the commencement of meetings of this committee being a result of the death of the late chairman of the committee. The hon. member should realize that one or two meetings of this committee were held at which time he could have ascertained that this committee was functioning with a new chairman. He would also have known that the clerk of that committee has been responsible for looking after the documents that were assembled. I might inform him at this time that the committee had the services of an economist during the holiday period for the purpose of assembling this material. This material has not gone to waste for want of a chairman. I might suggest that this committee could have taken the opportunity of meeting some months ago, if the house had directed it to do so. There has been ample time, during the last two or three months, to have conducted an investigation into the price of farm machinery. I believe a good deal could have been accomplished during the recess, and this committee would have been prepared to hold meetings to study this whole question of the increased cost of farm machinery.

I shall not delay any longer the discussion of this measure. I shall not dwell on the complaints made by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) in particular. In fact, he implied that farmers should continue to cultivate the soil with the type of implements used in 1920 or in 1925. No farmer would buy such outdated machinery, because we would be moving backwards if we were to limit the various models to what they were 10, 15 or 20 years ago. You have there a sample of what the administration would be like if, his party unfortunately, had to form a government and thus look after the future of the farm population across the country.

Farm Machinery Prices
I urge my colleagues and all members in this house to support this measure wholeheartedly since its objective is to help the farm people even more fairly.

speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize the Minister of Labour, with the approval of the governor in council, to enter into agreements with provinces to provide for the sharing of costs incurred by the provinces in carrying out programs of vocational rehabilitation for disabled persons; to authorize the minister to undertake the co-ordination of federal activities in the field of vocational rehabilitation and to undertake research in respect to vocational rehabilitation; and for those purposes to provide for the establishment of a council to be called the national advisory council on the rehabilitation of disabled persons; and to provide further for the payment of the chairman's remuneration and of the travelling and other expenses of the members thereof and for such professional, technical, secretarial and other assistance as the council may require.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Flynn in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES ETC.
PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES ETC.
speechtext:
I rise to indicate our support for the principle of this resolution, because we are convinced that any provision to promote and expand a program of vocational rehabilitation for disabled persons deserves the support of all hon. members.
Rehabilitation has as its aim the development and restoration of the disabled person to the fullest physical, metal, psycho-social, vocational and economic usefulness of which he is capable within the restrictions inherent in his environment. As the minister has already told us, rehabilitation has two main aspects. First, there is the human aspect, the enabling of the individual to live a useful, satisfying life and to make a useful contribution to society. Then there is the economic


aspect, to increase the economic productivity of the disabled persons and to enable them to contribute to the economy rather than to become a burden on the economy.
The increase in the life span of man which has been brought about by medical science has resulted in an increasingly large proportion of old people in our population who have to be supported by the working population. Between 1901 and 1949 the number of children under 15 years of age doubled, but during that same period the number of people over 45 trebled. There is a limit to the burden which the working population can carry, as well as to the standard of living which it can support. Anything, therefore, which can increase the working population and at the same time reduce the burden which the economy has to carry is a sound economic investment.
I have not been able to find up-to-date figures about the proportion of disabled people in Canada, but surveys carried out in the United States showed that the proportion of the disabled to the total population there was about 20 per thousand, not including disabled veterans. If we apply the same proportion to Canada, it would seem we have about 360,000 disabled persons in addition to our disabled veterans. In 1940 a very important experiment was carried out by the British ministry of labour in the United Kingdom. At that time they had 185,000 disabled men and women who were listed as unemployable, but as a result of that experiment that number was reduced to less than 8,000. That proves beyond doubt that 97 per cent of our disabled persons can be rehabilitated to the point where they can lead useful productive lives and that 80 per cent of our handicapped people of working age are capable of being rehabilitated into employment; that is, they can become economically useful without the benefit of highly specialized and expensive services.
As the minister pointed out this evening our experience with disabled war veterans in Canada has confirmed the result of that British experiment. I think those of us who have had the pleasure of visiting Sunnybrook hospital and other veteran centres have been amazed at the rehabilitation work which has been accomplished there. It is against this kind of background that we must discuss the resolution which is now before us.
The legislation which will be introduced as a result of this resolution seeks to achieve four main objectives. The first is to make agreements with the provinces with respect to cost sharing. The second is to co-ordinate federal activities and to carry out research. The third purpose is to set up a national advisory council on vocational rehabilitation, and the fourth is to equip this council with

the necessary staff and equipment and to make provision for salary and operating expenses. I should like to say a word about each of these objectives. In the first place with regard to the agreements with the provinces about cost sharing, may I say that the usual cost sharing agreement worked out between the provinces and the federal government has been on a fifty-fifty basis. That has not proved satisfactory to the poorer provinces because the poorer provinces such as Newfoundland can be ruined by cost sharing schemes. I think this resolution differs from most arrangements of this kind inasmuch as it involves human beings and I would hope that when the minister works out the agreements envisaged in his resolution they will be on a basis of need, and on the basis of the capacity of the province concerned to provide the facilities including trained personnel which are necessary to enable this program to be carried out successfully.
The co-ordination of federal activities is certainly a step in the right direction. At the moment rehabilitation activities are being carried on by the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Department of Labour and the Department of National Health and Welfare. At the provincial and municipal levels we have various provincial and municipal services. Much work is being done voluntarily by private agencies. I would hope that the federal example of co-ordinating the services would be followed by the provinces.
I take it that one of the reasons for this co-ordination is that people would have to deal only with the national advisory council which would serve as a clearing house or liaison for all the work that has to be done in this connection. It is not clear from what the minister said this evening whether the council will actually take over this work or whether it will continue to be carried on by the various departments but be co-ordinated by this body.
Of course, there is a great deal of research to be done in this connection. First of all we need statistical research to tell us how many people will be affected, what age groups they fall in, what categories of disabilities and handicaps are most prevalent in each age group and in addition there will have to be an examination of the research that has been done relating to the techniques and procedures that have been and are being developed in other countries. I presume there will be some co-ordination of the production of films, posters and publications in connection with rehabilitation that are put out by the various departments.
The third objective contained in this resolution is not a new idea. In 1951 a national
Vocational Rehabilitation conference on rehabilitation was sponsored by the Hon. Milton Gregg, who at that time was minister of labour. Also active in the sponsorship were Mr. Lapointe, the then minister of veterans affairs, and my colleague, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) who was then the minister of national health and welfare. Now that the government has embarked on an expanded program of rehabilitation perhaps the time has come to set up a permanent body.
While on this subject I should like to pay tribute to the work being done with respect to the rehabilitation of the disabled in my own province. I think in particular of the work being done by the tuberculosis association, by the orthopedic wing of the general hospital, by the children's rehabilitation centre and the sunshine camp for small children. The latter has played an important part in assisting the disabled children of poor people in the outlying areas, improving their health to the point where they have been able to undergo surgery and take treatment for their disability.
I also think of the work being done by the provincial branch of the institute for the blind and of the treatment provided to the deaf and dumb children. There is such a host of organizations and agencies engaged in important work of this nature that one hesitates to mention one for fear of overlooking another. I wish to pay tribute to all of them for the work they are doing and have done in my province.
The essence of a program of this nature is the placement service. There is no point in rehabilitating a disabled person and teaching him a trade if after he has learned a trade there is no work for him to do. That has been perhaps the greatest shortcoming in my own province. We have trained people as barbers, clockmakers, taught them to repair clocks, shoes and television sets, but there is no great demand for work of this nature and we cannot place all our disabled people in these trades.
I hope the federal government will develop a policy of giving preference to disabled persons. In my own province, before confederation, the government did have such a policy. It was an unwritten policy but was accepted by the people generally. In every small settlement there is usually someone with some physical disability, one who is crippled, who has impaired sight or who is handicapped in one way or other. Before we became a part of Canada if there was a position as postmaster vacant a disabled person was given preference because it was a job he could handle. We trained people for telegraph offices, for bookkeeping positions and other clerical

Vocational Rehabilitation jobs and under the unwritten policy, disabled persons were given preference.
Since we joined Canada a different policy has been pursued by the federal government and many of these jobs that used to be set aside for the disabled are no longer available. I think it was a good policy and if, when it is set up, the council is going to coordinate all these activities I hope it will develop a policy of giving preference to disabled persons and that this policy will be adopted by the federal government.
Even a policy of this nature will not provide jobs for all our disabled people in a province such as mine where the population is widely scattered in may small communities. One way of solving the problem, and at the same time of making a contribution to the economy, would be for the council to sponsor home industries and handicrafts which will enable disabled people to work in their own homes making some product that has a market value that can be sold to provide an income for the disabled person and his family. It will probably be necessary to establish a national organization of some description to market these products.
We have people of tremendous talent in many of our small settlements. In the words of the old adage, many a rose is born to blush unseen. In our small settlements we have people with a great ability to paint, singers and musicians and people who are skilled in many handicrafts. This I think would be a solution in a sparsely populated province, and possibly it would apply to the maritimes as well as to Newfoundland.
We know from the work that has been done by the Newfoundland outport nurses' association and by the Grenfell mission that there is a demand for handicrafts of high quality. These groups sponsored the purchase of looms so that handicapped people could weave cloth and make knitted goods. The goods were of high quality and found a ready market.
I pass on these suggestions to the minister because the whole program stands or falls on our ability to find some method of providing work for these people after they are trained.
I conclude, Mr. Chairman, in the hope that this expanded program will be successful and that it will contribute greatly to the productivity of our disabled population.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister introduced this resolution and the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo followed. Both spoke about the principles behind this particular resolution. I have to agree wholeheartedly with them. The principles upon which this resolution is based are indeed very good ones. But I do not think it is good enough to

bring in a resolution based upon good principles unless we are going to adopt some of those principles and put them to some use. From reading the resolution itself, from listening to the presentation made by the minister and from the information he has provided us so far, I am not too sure just how much good is going to come from this particular resolution.
First of all, the minister said it is to encourage action and it so states in the resolution. The purpose is to permit the federal government to enter into agreements with the provinces to provide for the sharing of costs incurred by the provinces in carrying out programs of vocational rehabilitation of disabled persons, and so on. While it is true that the resolution is based on good principles and it is a nice gesture in the right direction, nevertheless the initiative has been left completely with the provinces. We have no assurance that after the passage of this resolution the condition will be any better in the future than it has been in the past.
The minister went on to say that the purpose was to bring hope, to the disabled. Again, this is quite a true statement so far as it goes. It brought hope to me when I saw the resolution on the order paper. I really thought we were going to get our teeth into the problem and do something more about it than we had been doing in the past. Apparently that is not so, because toward the end of his remarks I noticed the minister said that there would be no new expenditures, no further expenditures in the future on the part of the federal government than there have been in the past. While the introduction of this resolution may bring hope to the disabled, I would remind the hon. member and the minister and the other hon. members that it takes more than hope to buy groceries.
The minister said something about a practical and vigorous program. I believe these were some of his words. I did not get them all down; unfortunately, I cannot write shorthand. Again these are fine words, but the minister failed to indicate any kind of practical or vigorous program which he was going to embark upon as a result of this particular resolution.
The minister went on to say further that the plans up to date and the methods adopted in the past, particularly on the part of the federal government, have been experimental ones. While it has been an experimental plan up to date, if we are to embark on a practical and vigorous program and at the same time confine ourselves to the same amount of money we have been putting into this scheme in the past, I do not see how the resolution will mean anything more than some more window dressing.

Business of the House
The minister quoted a host of statistics. He mentioned 5,266 seriously disabled people who come under this plan, 80 per cent of them formerly without earnings. He went on to say that actual earnings amount to $9 million and the welfare costs came to $3 million. He did not say what their earnings were before, or what the cost of the upkeep is now. Therefore, statistics of this kind which give only one side of the picture are not really very useful.
I have some further remarks to make on this matter but I see the hour of ten has approached. Will you call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman?
